summary: Reflects on RFC 1591 and how IANA and ICANN might have interpreted it for domain categories in today's world. It is published mainly for historical context and comparison. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a thoughtful essay about the old rules for who gets which kind of website ending, and how they could have been applied differently.

questions: should country domains follow icann rules
what is the purpose of ccTLDs
subtitle: Reconsideration of domain allocation policies in a post-web internet.

tldr.problem: RFC 1591 laid out principles for domain allocation when the internet was small and the web did not exist. As the internet grew exponentially, domain names became valuable, pressure mounted to change the rules, and IANA/ICANN drifted from RFC 1591's original philosophy without always understanding why those principles existed.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes a refined three-category system to replace RFC 1591's binary split: generic TLDs (anyone), purpose-specific TLDs (qualified registrants), and country domains (domestic use). Each category would have appropriate ICANN involvement: minimal for country domains, full for generic TLDs, selective for purpose-specific ones.
tldr.outcome: The RFC documents why RFC 1591's safeguards—avoiding sovereignty disputes, preventing judgments about government legitimacy, mediating rather than judging—remain sound even as domain demand and commercialization changed.

today: RFC 3071 is Informational and is published primarily for historical context. It documents John Klensin's thoughts on how RFC 1591's principles might have guided a more coherent ICANN policy during a period of significant debate about domain policy direction.

sections.title: RFC 1591 and Internet Growth
sections.content:
RFC 1591, written by Jon Postel in 1994, established the foundational principles for allocating and managing top-level domains. It assumed generic TLDs (like COM, NET, ORG) would be policy-bound and relatively restricted, while country-code TLDs (ccTLDs) would serve residents of their countries. The design reflected a philosophy that domain administration was a public service, not a profit center.

The internet has changed dramatically since 1591 was written. The World Wide Web put domain names directly in front of users, making them visible and desirable. The number of hosts increased; more importantly, the ratio of registered domain names to physical hosts increased very significantly. Domain names became valuable assets, spawning secondary markets, disputes over valuable addresses, and pressure on ICANN to relax restrictions.

Many subsequent debates and policy changes cited RFC 1591, sometimes correctly and sometimes based on misconceptions about what it actually said or why. ICANN's policies began drifting away from the original philosophy—not necessarily wrongly, but without reconstructing or explaining why 1591's safeguards existed. This document proposes that some of RFC 1591's principles remain sound and could guide a refined categorization system.
sections.plainLanguage: Old rules worked when the internet was small and domain names were not valuable. Once domain names became desirable, everyone wanted a piece, and the rules started to break. This is a thoughtful look at how to adjust those old rules to work in today's world.

sections.title: A Three-Category System
sections.content:
This RFC proposes replacing RFC 1591's implicit two-way split with a more explicit three-way categorization:

  • Generic TLDs: COM, NET, ORG, and similar domains where any registration is acceptable and registrations are actively promoted. Anyone can register (subject to name conflicts and local law), without qualification.
  • Purpose-Specific TLDs: INT (infrastructure), EDU (education), ARPA, and US Government domains (MIL, GOV), plus newer sponsored TLDs such as specialized domains for medical entities or museums. Registration requires meeting specific qualifications (e.g., being an educational institution for EDU), but qualification is not tied to national boundaries.
  • Country Domains: ccTLDs operated as true country services, where registrants are expected to be people or entities within the country. External registrations may be accepted but are not aggressively marketed, and the domain does not derive significant revenue from outside registrations.

Importantly, these categories are separate from the ISO 3166 country-code system. A ccTLD can be either a country domain or operate as a generic domain. The key distinction is operational style, not which letter code was assigned.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of asking 'is this generic or a country domain?' ask 'is it open to anyone, or to people in one country, or to people with specific qualifications?' The answer tells you how to run it and what rules apply.

sections.title: ICANN's Role and Domain Autonomy
sections.content:
True country domains (category iii) should operate with minimal ICANN involvement once delegated, assuming an administrative contact in the country is always available. They may choose to adopt ICANN dispute resolution policies or handle disputes under national law. They should only pay ICANN for services they use, not for general administration of the root and root servers.

Generic-operated ccTLDs should follow standard ICANN policies for dispute resolution, name management, and multi-registrar oversight, just like COM and NET do.

Purpose-specific TLDs need careful definition but fall between the two extremes. Self-identification is key: a ccTLD should be able to clearly state whether it operates as a generic domain (actively seeking external registrations) or as a country domain (primarily internal). Criteria for distinction include aggressive marketing practices, percentage of in-country registrants, and whether the administrative contact and registrants are likely to be subject to the country's jurisdiction and laws.

All domains should be required to publish their intended policies (dispute resolution, registration rules, etc.) so registrants know what they are entering into. Giving IANA incorrect information about a domain's intended use should be subject to challenge and grounds for reviewing the domain delegation.
sections.plainLanguage: If a domain is really for a country, it should mostly leave ICANN alone and be left alone. If it acts like a global domain, it should follow global rules. Each domain should say upfront how it works.

sections.title: Why This Matters: Avoiding Political Entanglement
sections.content:
IANA's original strategy for ccTLDs included three critical "things to avoid": (1) never determine which entities are countries; (2) never determine who is the legitimate government of a country; (3) avoid deciding disputes within a country except as a mediator.

These principles aimed to keep IANA and ICANN out of political and diplomatic tangles where they have no competence. IANA accomplished this by strictly adhering to the ISO 3166 country-code list: if an entity had a code, it was eligible; if not, the applicant's recourse was the ISO Maintenance Agency, not IANA. Only five exceptions to this rule exist (UK, and Ascension Island, Guernsey, Isle of Man, Jersey), and the author argues they should be acknowledged as mistakes rather than precedents.

Under the proposed model, ccTLDs operating as country domains would face less ICANN pressure to harmonize globally. Governments that wish to assert control can do so by influencing the administrative contact to request delegation changes, naturally establishing legitimacy through practical ability to assert pressure. This avoids ICANN needing to judge government authenticity. By contrast, ccTLDs marketed as generic domains would properly fall under ICANN's governance structure.

The RFC reflects deep skepticism about ICANN's ability and mandate to make international political or governance decisions, and advocates minimizing those entanglements where possible.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA invented a clever trick: use ISO country codes so you never have to decide who is a 'real' country. If a government wants to control its domain, it can pressure the person in charge of that domain. This avoids IANA becoming a judge of international politics, which it was never supposed to do.

references.text: Postel, J., "Domain Name System Structure and Delegation", RFC 1591, March 1994.
